summary: Presents High Capacity Textual Conventions for MIB modules that need performance history based on 15 minute intervals. They extend the conventions in RFC 3593 to 64-bit resolution using the conventions in RFC 2856. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Counters keeping track of things every 15 minutes can fill up too fast on busy equipment. This gives bigger counters so they do not overflow.

questions: high capacity textual conventions 15 minute intervals
what are textual conventions in a mib
why are performance history intervals 15 minutes
subtitle: 64-bit counter types for MIB modules that keep performance history in 15-minute buckets.

tldr.problem: Telecom equipment keeps performance history in 15-minute intervals, and the existing 32-bit textual conventions in RFC 3593 are too small for high-capacity counts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3705 defines a MIB module of textual conventions built directly on the Counter64 type, plus a few small integer conventions for interval bookkeeping, following the approach of RFC 2856.
tldr.outcome: The conventions are explicitly described as a limited and short-term solution that may be deprecated once a long-term solution is defined and deployed.

today: RFC 3705 is a Proposed Standard from February 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says the conventions may be deprecated once a long-term solution is defined and deployed.

sections.title: Performance History in 15-Minute Buckets
sections.content:
A manager that wants performance history from managed equipment can follow two strategies. The agent can count events continuously and let the manager read the counter and work out the history. Or the agent can allocate events to buckets, each representing an interval of time.

Telecommunications equipment often uses the bucket strategy, and the standard practice is to keep history in 15-minute intervals. MIB modules built this way already exist for DS1/E1, DS3/E3, SONET/SDH, ADSL, HDSL2 and SHDSL interfaces. They share the textual conventions of RFC 3593.
sections.eli5: Instead of one giant running tally, the equipment keeps a fresh little tally for every 15 minutes, like a new page in a notebook each quarter hour.

sections.title: Why 64 Bits and Why Counter64
sections.content:
A need arose for 64-bit versions of the RFC 3593 conventions. A Gauge64 or Unsigned64 type would be ideal, but SMIv2 has neither. Basing them on the CounterBasedGauge64 convention from RFC 2856 is not possible either, because SMIv2 allows only base types when defining a textual convention. So these conventions are built directly on Counter64.

That choice brings four limits on objects that use them:

  • MAX-ACCESS must be read-only.
  • No sub-range can be specified.
  • No DEFVAL clause can be specified.
  • They cannot be used in an INDEX clause.
sections.eli5: The rulebook has no ready-made big plain number, so the authors borrow a big counter and live with its rules: you can read it, but you cannot set it or use it as a label.

sections.title: What the Agent Must Provide
sections.content:
Using these conventions assumes four things about the agent:

  • It supports 15-minute based history counters.
  • It can keep a history of 96 intervals of 15-minute data.
  • It may optionally support performance data that aggregates the history intervals.
  • It keeps separate tables for the current interval, the history intervals and the total aggregates.
sections.eli5: The equipment needs to keep 96 old pages, one page for right now, and optionally a running grand total, each in its own notebook.

sections.title: The Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module HC-PerfHist-TC-MIB is registered as mib-2 107 and defines these conventions.

Three small integer conventions describe the bookkeeping:

  • HCPerfValidIntervals (Integer32, 0..96) is the number of intervals with data. It is 96 unless measurement was (re)started within the last 1440 minutes.
  • HCPerfInvalidIntervals (Integer32, 0..96) is the number of intervals with no data, typically zero except in cases such as proxies.
  • HCPerfTimeElapsed (Integer32, 0..86399) is the seconds since the current measurement period began. For 15-minute intervals the range is limited to 0..899.

HCPerfIntervalThreshold (Unsigned32, 0..900) sets a fault threshold alarm control, where 0 disables the alarm.

Three Counter64 conventions hold the counts. HCPerfCurrentCount is the gauge for the current interval. HCPerfIntervalCount is the gauge for a previous interval. HCPerfTotalCount is the aggregate of previous valid intervals, and intervals with no valid data are not counted.
sections.eli5: There are small number types for bookkeeping, such as how many pages are filled in and how many seconds have passed. There are also three big counter types: one for now, one for each old page, and one for the grand total.

sections.title: How the Counts Roll Over
sections.content:
The current count starts from zero and rises as events occur until the interval ends. Its value is then stored in the first history interval and the gauge restarts at zero. If the agent has no valid data for an interval, that object instance is not available and a retrieval returns an error saying the instance does not exist.

For history intervals X(1) to X(n), where X(1) is the most recent, the end of each 15-minute interval works like this: the value of X(n) is discarded, each X(i) takes the value of X(i-1), X(1) takes the value of the current count, and the total, if supported, is adjusted.

All three counts are non-negative, may increase or decrease, and never exceed 2^64-1 (18446744073709551615) or fall below 0. If the underlying count exceeds the maximum, the object holds the maximum. If the underlying count later falls back, for example after a retroactive adjustment for unavailable time, the object's value falls too.
sections.eli5: When 15 minutes end, the current page goes to the top of the stack, every older page moves down one, and the oldest page falls off. The counter sticks at its biggest value rather than wrapping to zero.

sections.title: Caveats and Security
sections.content:
Each count convention carries a warning. It is not strictly supported in SMIv2, because the always-increasing and counter-wrap semantics of Counter64 are not preserved. A management application that relies only on the Counter64 ASN.1 tag may wrongly treat these objects like ordinary Counter64 objects. The text calls the conventions a limited and short-term solution that may be deprecated when a long-term solution is defined and deployed.

On security, the module defines no management objects, only conventions for other MIB modules to use. The RFC states that meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define the objects, so it has no impact on the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: These big counters act a little differently from real counters, so programs must not assume they behave the same. The authors say this is a stopgap.
